turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr Pillay, do come in and have a seat. The sister has clipped a note to your file, so I have seen the figures, but I would rather hear from you what brought you in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I came chiefly to have a form completed for my employer, and I thought I might mention the knee while I was here.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): We can do both. Tell me about the knee first, and then we will come to the form and to what the sister found.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It is the right knee. It has been stiff, and a little sore, since I slipped on a wet pavement. I cannot give you an exact date, I am afraid. It was sometime after the Easter long weekend, but I would not like to be pinned down.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): That is all right. We can leave the date open. Was it swollen at the time, and does it swell now?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It was a bit puffy for a few days at the beginning, and then that settled. It is not swollen now. The stairs at the office make it complain, and it is stiff after I have been sitting in the car.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And what do you do for it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I take Panado, by mouth. Two of the five hundred milligram tablets, when it is properly sore. That would be about twice a week, not every day. It does ease it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two Panado, five hundred milligrams each, by mouth, about twice a week, for the knee. You are not on anything else regularly?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor, not now. About five-ish years ago a pharmacy screening said the pressure was up, and a doctor there gave me a water tablet to take once a day. I think it was twenty milligrams, though I am not certain of the strength, and I took it for about a month and then stopped because I felt quite well.

[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the water tablet was stopped after about a month, and you cannot recall the proper name, only that it was a water tablet, perhaps twenty milligrams. You are not taking it now.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct. My sister is forever offering me her biotin capsules, which she takes for her hair. I have never taken them, and I do not intend to start.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): We will leave your sister's biotin out of your list entirely. Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I know of, Doctor. I have been fortunate in that regard.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. With these pressure readings I do need to ask a few things. Any headaches, chest pain, change in your vision, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No headaches, Doctor. No chest pain. My vision is perfectly all right, and I am not short of breath.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): The sister wrote one hundred and seventy-six over one hundred and two on the first check.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I do apologise, that sounds dreadful. It is the white coat, I am quite sure. I was flustered. The parking this side of the rooms was full, and the robot on Voortrekker was out with the load shedding, so I arrived rather wound up.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): She repeated it a few minutes later and got a hundred and sixty-four over ninety-six. Still up, though not the same numbers. Your pulse on her note is seventy-eight.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Even so, Doctor, at the pharmacy machine it is always fine. I have not written the figures down, I must admit. I simply glance and feel reassured.

[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): So we have two clinic readings, both raised, and a feeling that the pharmacy readings are normal, without a record. I am not going to call this a definite diagnosis today.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I would be grateful if we did not rush into tablets. My wife is on metformin for her sugar, two tablets a day, but that is entirely hers. I do not take sugar tablets, and I have never had sugar trouble.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Metformin is your wife's, not yours, and I will not record it on your list. You have not had diabetes yourself. Is that right?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Quite so. My late father had a stroke, shame, when he was seventy-odd. He was a heavy smoker, which I am not. I only mention it because these pressure numbers made me think of him.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am sorry about your father. So there is a stroke in the family, on your father's side, and he smoked. You yourself have never smoked.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. A glass of wine with supper on a Saturday, sometimes a Sunday, and nothing more. I work in accounts at the municipality, desk work, and I stay in Westdene with my wife.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back. Never smoked, a glass of wine at the weekend, a desk job in municipal accounts, and you live with your wife in Westdene. Any operations in the past?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Only my appendix, as a young man, in the eighties. Nothing since.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Appendix in the nineteen eighties, and nothing after that. How are the waterworks and the bowels, and are you sleeping all right?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Waterworks are fine, bowels are regular, and I sleep well enough. The neighbour's dog has opinions at five in the morning, but that is hardly medical.

[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will leave the dog out of the notes. On the right knee there is no swelling I can see, it bends fully, and there is a little crepitus as you straighten it. The joint line is not particularly tender.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): That pressure is uncomfortable, but not sharp. It feels much the same as when I climb the stairs.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I am not going to repeat the blood pressure myself this minute. Two readings are enough to act on, and a third in this room may not settle the white coat question.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): If I may ask, does this mean tablets today? I am rather hoping the form can still be signed. It is only a fitness declaration for desk duty.

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): No blood pressure tablets today. I would like home readings before any medicine is considered. My impression, and it is only an impression, is that this may be white coat hypertension, though sustained hypertension is still quite possible.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): That matches what I have thought. Though, um, I should correct something I said earlier, if I may.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please do.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I said I have no headaches. That was too quick of me. Most mornings this week I have woken with a dull ache across the forehead. It is not severe, and it settles once I have had tea.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for coming back to that. So there is a mild morning headache across the forehead, most mornings this past week, and it eases after tea. The chest pain, the shortness of breath, and the vision, do those still stand as absent?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, and no visual change, even with the headache. I have not felt weak or faint.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will hold those as absent, and I will record the headache as present. It does not by itself prove that the pressure is the cause, but I would not ignore it.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. Should I be worried about a stroke, given my father?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not on today's findings alone. There is no weakness and no sudden visual loss. We simply should not leave the pressure unmeasured at home.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): What would you like me to do, then?

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will arrange a home blood pressure monitor from the clinic. Please use it morning and evening for seven days, sitting quietly, and write every figure in the little book. Bring it to me in two weeks.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning and evening for seven days, and back in two weeks. I can manage that. Do I use the right arm or the left? My father had a rather ancient machine, but I never learned it.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Either arm is acceptable if you keep to the same one. The left is usual. Sit for five minutes first, and do not check it straight after climbing the hill.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): The hill past the robot, yes. I walk that most mornings, from the parking. It is the only exercise I get, I am afraid, apart from the stairs.

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Walking most mornings is worth keeping up. On the knee, I do not see a need for an x-ray today. If it has not settled in six weeks, we might arrange an x-ray of the right knee then.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): I am content with that. May I carry on with the Panado as I have been taking it?

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Carry on with the Panado as you described, two five hundred milligram tablets by mouth when the knee is sore. If the pain becomes severe, or the knee locks or gives way, come back sooner rather than waiting for those six weeks.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): And the salt, and the coffee? At the office I drink rather a lot of coffee, four cups a day. I wondered if that was pushing the pressure up.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ease the coffee back if you can, and keep the salt modest. That is advice, not a tablet. We are not starting blood pressure treatment today, even with the headache now on the table.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall try. Four cups is a habit from month-end, when the accounts close. I will cut it down.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me summarise, and do stop me if I have anything wrong. You came for an employer fitness form, and for a right knee that has been sore and stiff since sometime after Easter, date uncertain. Early puffiness has gone, and the Panado helps.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct so far.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): You are on no regular medicine. A water tablet, proper name unknown, perhaps twenty milligrams, was stopped after about a month, five-ish years ago. Your wife takes metformin and your sister takes biotin, and you take neither.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. And it is the right knee. I had a moment's worry that the notes might say left, but you have it right.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right knee, thank you. Your father had a stroke. You have never smoked, and the wine is weekends only.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor.

[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): No allergies, no chest pain, no breathlessness, and no visual change. You do have a mild morning headache this past week. The two pressures were one hundred and seventy-six over one hundred and two, and a hundred and sixty-four over ninety-six, with a pulse of seventy-eight.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): They are quite far apart, are they not? Which one do you believe?

[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): I believe both were real when they were taken. The difference is why a home series will serve us better than choosing a favourite number today. I am not certain yet whether this is white coat hypertension or sustained hypertension.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): I see. And if the home figures are high?
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the home readings stay high, then we might start a blood pressure tablet at the next visit. I will not name one today, and I am not prescribing one now.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): That is a relief, if I may say so. What of the form? My supervisor asked for it this week, if possible.

[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will complete the form just now, before you leave. I will say the knee does not stop you doing desk work, and that the blood pressure is being checked at home and is not yet on treatment.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): I would prefer accuracy. Thank you. Is there anything I should bring besides the book of readings?

[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring the book, and the monitor if we have loaned it, so we can look at the machine together. If you feel a sudden severe headache, weakness, chest pain, or breathlessness before then, do not wait the two weeks.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall come straight in, or go to casualty at the provincial hospital if the rooms are shut. I hope it will not come to that.

[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): Quite. One more check on the old water tablet, so the notes stay honest. You said perhaps twenty milligrams, and you were not sure. Shall I leave the strength as an uncertain twenty, or is another figure coming back to you?

[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): Please leave it uncertain. I nearly said twelve and a half just now, but that would be a guess upon a guess. I truly do not know the strength, and the name is gone. It was only ever the water tablet to me.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I will not invent a name or a firm dose. Discontinued, dose uncertain, taken for about a month, around five-ish years ago. It is not a current medicine.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): I am grateful you are being so careful. The waiting room was rather full, and I hope I have not taken too much of your morning.

[SEG0075] person_1 (DOCTOR): You have not. Home monitor arranged, readings for seven days, back in two weeks, no new tablets today, the form to be done before you leave, and an x-ray only if the knee is still troublesome in six weeks. The receptionist can book the review as you go out.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I shall collect the form and the monitor on my way out. Good morning to you.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

bad.reason: Wife's sugar is her condition, not the patient's family history entry stated here.
Water tablet, once daily, about a month, five-ish years ago supported; 20 mg is uncertain, not definite.
bad.text: water tablet (dose=20 mg, frequency=once a day, duration=approximately 1 month, stopped approximately 5 years ago, indication=raised blood pressure, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Recorded family history is wrong: the wife being on metformin for her sugar is not the patient's family history/medical history; it was explicitly stated to be his wife's medication and not his condition.
Panado current dose is incompletely recorded: he takes two 500 mg tablets by mouth when sore, i.e. a total of 1000 mg per dose, about twice a week.

The discontinued 'water tablet' dose is recorded too definitively as 20 mg; the patient said the strength was uncertain and specifically asked that it remain uncertain, even mentioning 12.5 mg would only be a guess.
Negative finding omitted: no headaches was initially denied before the patient corrected himself later.
Negative findings omitted: no weakness and no sudden visual loss were specifically noted by the doctor when discussing stroke concern/red flags.
Negative finding omitted: no knee locking or giving way currently; these were discussed as warning symptoms to return earlier if they occur.
History omitted: prior pharmacy machine blood pressure readings were said by the patient to be 'always fine', but he has not written the figures down.

Plan detail omitted: home blood pressure monitor is to be loaned/arranged from the clinic, with readings morning and evening for 7 days after sitting quietly for 5 minutes, using the same arm each time (left usual), and avoiding checking straight after exertion.
Follow-up detail omitted: bring the blood pressure record book and the monitor itself to the review visit so the machine can be checked together.
Review-of-systems negative omitted: bowels regular and waterworks fine are recorded, but the patient also said he sleeps well enough.
